entries.title: Weakened US fuel-efficiency rules and promises of cheaper cars could see drivers pay higher running costs while also increasing carbon emissions.
entries.summary: Weakened US fuel-efficiency rules and promises of cheaper cars could yet see drivers pay higher running costs while increasing planet-heating emissions.
entries.content:
October 1, 2026

Weakened US fuel-efficiency rules and promises of cheaper cars could yet see drivers pay higher running costs while increasing planet-heating emissions.

As part of its "Freedom Means More Affordable Cars" initiative, the US Department of Transportation this week rolled back fuel efficiency rules under the guise of lowering vehicle prices.

The Trump administration's transport agency says US taxpayers will save $138 billion (€122 billion) over the next five years — new vehicles will be $1,300 cheaper on average — since automakers will no longer have to invest in more fuel-efficient fleets.

But this does not account for soaring gas prices as Middle East conflicts choke global supply. 

"Any savings on the front end get eaten up and spat out by excess costs of fuel … Fuel economy standards have saved drivers hundreds of billions of dollars," said Democratic Senator Sheldon Whitehouse in a social media post.

Under the revised Corporate Average Fuel Economy (CAFE) rules, vehicle fleets only require an average fuel efficiency of about 35 miles per gallon (14.7km per liter) by 2031, down around one-third from 50 miles per gallon.



Implemented by the Biden administration in 2024, the updated efficiency rules aimed to incentivize the production of low emission electric vehicles and hybrids. The US National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) estimates the standards would have saved 70 billion gallons (265 billion litres) of fuel over 25 years. 

Meanwhile, nonprofit advocacy group, the Union of Concerned Scientists (UCS) says an earlier version of CAFE regulations has saved US consumers have saved about $321 billion at the gas pump since 2010.

Rollbacks set to increase planet-heating emissions

The world's biggest petrol consumer, the US burns through 20 million barrels of oil per day, which is 20% of global consumption, notes Dan Becker, director of the Safe Climate Transport Campaign at the US-based nonprofit environmental group Center for Biological Diversity.

"Transportation is the biggest consumer of that oil, making strong auto standards the most effective way to cut pollution and oil use," Becker said in a statement.

The rules that have been diluted this week would have prevented more than 710 million metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions by 2050 — the equivalent of running 165 million gas-powered passenger vehicles for a year.

"With transportation representing nearly 28% of US greenhouse emissions, rolling back fuel economy standards is a dangerous setback for near-term climate goals," said Ben Scott, head of Energy Demand at UK-based climate think tank, Carbon Tracker.



"It risks keeping inefficient combustion engines on the road much longer than climate science demands," he told DW. 

But following the Trump administration’s elimination of greenhouse gas emissions standards for light- and heavy-duty vehicles last year, Dave Cooke, senior vehicles analyst for the UCS Clean Transportation Program, said the rollbacks merely compound "a much more significant step backwards."

He said the trend sends "a specific signal to automakers," adding that "the United States is seeking to maximize oil usage to increase oil company profits."

This will be to the detriment of climate targets, with high-polluting oil contributing one-third of global fossil fuel emissions that continue to rise — along with temperatures.

The world just had the hottest August on record as severe heatwaves in Europe caused over 16,000 excess deaths in Germany alone.  

Can US transport still transition to clean energy?

Sales of low emission EVs are down in the US in 2026, especially after president Trump scrapped the $7,500 tax credit for new electric vehicles.  

American automakers also continue to push back against regulations that would incentivize a switch to EVs, arguing there is a lack of consumer demand. 

"It's highly unlikely that the United States will suddenly become awash in electric options when neither the auto industry nor regulators seem interested in providing such choices for consumers," said Cooke.

But Ben Scott believes that while softening US fuel economy standards "will create temporary headwinds", it won't stall an inevitable transition to electric vehicles.

"With EVs delivering vastly lower running costs, electrification becomes a clear-cut economic choice," he said of cars running on "cheaper, domestically secure energy that will drive the transition forward, regardless of short-term politics."

As less efficient cars and trucks consume more oil that's more expensive and in shorter supply, "the fragility of oil-dependent transport" is set to be exposed, he said.



Edited by: Tamsin Walker

entries.title: UAE launches flydubai hijacking and terrorism investigation
entries.summary: The UAE's chief prosecutor said it's looking at the possibility of "terrorist activity or intent" in the alleged attempted hijacking of a flydubai commercial flight to Tel Aviv. It says it has jurisdiction in the case.
entries.content:
October 1, 2026

The UAE's chief prosecutor said it's looking at the possibility of "terrorist activity or intent" in the alleged attempted hijacking of a flydubai commercial flight to Tel Aviv. It says it has jurisdiction in the case.

The United Arab Emirates' chief prosecutor's office said on Thursday that it had ordered an investigation into the apparent attempt to hijack and possibly crash a flydubai flight to Israel a day earlier. 

The state news agency WAM said that "the investigation team has launched its work into the incident already" and that the probe would seek to determine "the degree to which [the incident] was linked to any terrorist activity or intent."

The case will also seek to establish whether it was a pre-meditated and planned incident involving other actors or the work of a lone perpetrator.

Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz had called the emergency on the flight to Tel Aviv "an attempted jihadist terror attack" that was thwarted. 

Passengers described rushing the cockpit to assist the pilot after he was stabbed by his copilot, who then put the plane into a steep dive in an apparent attempt to crash the airliner.

Aside from minor cuts and bruises among those who intervened in the cockpit, the passengers — the vast majority of whom were Israeli — were all unhurt.

Why does the UAE have jurisdiction in the case?

Judicial authorities in the UAE have jurisdiction over the incident.

This is because the aircraft is registered in the UAE and flies under its flag, the statement said, adding that UAE law applied to crimes committed on board "even if they occur outside the country's territory."

The plane was over northern Saudi Arabia for the majority of the early-morning security incident, with tracking data suggesting it briefly crossed into Jordan before turning around to make an emergency landing at the nearby Tabuk Airport in Saudi Arabia. 

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had also indicated the likelihood of the UAE leading any investigation in a TV interview with Fox News. 

"The attacking pilot is ... now being investigated in Saudi Arabia. I think he'll be taken to the Emirates, where he comes from, or at least where he left, where he flew off from, and we'll be following and possibly also participating in this investigation," Netanyahu said.

The Omani copilot's identity has not been made public as yet and his motive is not clear. US President Donald Trump said that based on a discussion with Netanyahu, he understood that the suspect was "perhaps a terrorist or perhaps a whack-job."

Asked about the possibility of Iranian involvement amid the conflict in the Gulf, Netanyahu said "it's too early to say." 

Israel's Herzog nominates 4 passengers for presidential medal

Israeli President Isaac Herzog plans to nominate four passengers who helped overpower the attacker for the Presidential Medal for Civil Courage.

Herzog and Netanyahu spoke with the passengers when they arrived at Ben Gurion Airport on a replacement flight late on Wednesday.

Herzog named the passengers as Yaniv Hayoun, Shota Musayev, Zvika Manes and Asaf Rajuan.

"You put yourselves at risk to save others and prevented a terrible disater," Herzog said. "Today, the whole world saw the beautiful and courageous face of Israeli society."

The medal is Israel's highest civilian award for heroism. Herzog confers the medal but typically nominees are formally chosen by a committee.

Musayev, a dentist who administered first aid to the severely wounded Indian pilot, told Herzog everyone on board had acted courageously.

"We supported one another on the plane and also when we arrived in Saudi Arabia, and we took care of each other as we should," he said.

The Indian captain, Smit Machchhar, has also received staunch praise from Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu and from India's Narendra Modi. Passengers described how the pilot fought off his attacker despite his wounds and was able to open the cockpit door to let them in to aid him. He was in a stable condition in a Saudi hospital, India's Embassy in Riyadh said on Wednesday.

"In the face of the gravest danger and despite being seriously injured, he showed immense courage and an unwavering resolve to protect the lives of others," Modi said online. "His valor helped save hundreds of lives and avert a great tragedy."

Edited by: Elizabeth Schumacher

entries.title: Germans' biggest fear is the high cost of living, an annual study finds
entries.summary: What do Germans fear most in 2026? Wars? Global crises? Wrong. Their biggest concern is the cost of living, which keeps rising.
entries.content:
Germany

Germans' biggest fear is the high cost of living

October 1, 2026

What do Germans fear most in 2026? Wars? Global crises? Wrong. Their biggest concern is the cost of living, which keeps rising.

People in Germany are more politically engaged than they have been in a long time. This was also evident in the high voter turnout in the September state elections in Saxony-Anhalt, Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.

Germans are passionately debating immigration, the upcoming reforms to pensions, healthcare and long-term care, as well as democracy and the rule of law.

But by far their greatest fear is the cost of living in Germany, which is becoming increasingly expensive. At least, that is the finding of the 2026 study on "Germans' Fears," which the insurer R+V presented in Berlin.

From early May through late July of this year, researchers surveyed some 2,400 German-speaking citizens aged 14 and older.

The cost of living is again their top concern, as it has been in the survey for many years in a row. This study has been conducted annually since the early 1990s.

Last year, 52% of those polled cited the rising cost of daily life as their greatest concern; in 2026, that figure has risen to 59%.

At a press conference in Berlin, Isabelle Borucki, a political scientist from Marburg who served as a consultant on the study, explained why.

"The price of key items — energy, housing and food — has risen noticeably. This reduces the financial leeway for leisure, vacations and purchases. People can afford less and less."

Germans worry about higher taxes and contributions

The study also shows that people are well aware that Germany's social security systems are in a serious crisis. Both the state pension fund and long-term care insurance are chronically in the red.

Most people also seem to realize that taxes and contributions will rise. That is why the fear of higher taxes is stronger than in previous years.

"Behind the fear of higher taxes and benefit cuts lies the question of fairness, with people wondering who will bear the costs of modernization," Borucki said. "And they worry, 'Can I still rely on getting benefits I am entitled to?'"

Less fear of war, immigration and Donald Trump

But what about the issues that are also dominating the headlines in Germany? What about immigration and the increasing polarization of society? Or global upheavals?

A narrow majority of 52% of those surveyed fear that the number of refugees is overwhelming the German state. This fear ranks third among all concerns.

But when it comes to global upheavals, Germans are not so concerned.

Only 45% of respondents fear that US President Donald Trump's policies are making the world a more dangerous place, researcher Grischa Brower-Rabinowitsch said.

"That's significantly fewer than during his first term."

In 2018, during Trump's first term, 69% responded to the same question by saying that this made them very afraid. "After years of constant geopolitical alarm bells, people are starting to get used to it," Brower-Rabinowitsch said.

German politicians got poor grades

This trend also seems to hold true for other areas of concern: Germans are looking to the future with considerably less anxiety than expected. Only 34% now fear a war involving Germany, down from 41% last year.

Since 1992, the study has asked people if they are afraid of losing their job? Currently, only 20% of the surveyed members of the working population answered "yes." That is the lowest figure ever recorded.

However, the assessment of politicians — both those in the government and those in the opposition — is sobering: Respondents were asked to grade politicians with one being the best and six the worst (the grading system used at German schools). The result was an average score of 4.1, which is barely a passing mark.

Political scientist Borucki places the primary responsibility on the current government of conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) under Chancellor Friedrich Merz which came to power in May 2025.

After the end of the previous coalition government, many associated the new coalition with hopes for more leadership, less conflict and a rapid economic turnaround.

"That has not come to pass," says Borucki. "There is now a gap between the grand announcements and tangible results. People are disappointed and losing confidence."

This article was originally written in German.

entries.title: Pakistan launches deadly airstrikes on Afghanistan
entries.summary: The Taliban government in Afghanistan said at least nine civilians were killed in Pakistani airstrikes on two provinces overnight. Pakistan said it had struck militant hideouts, killing 22 fighters.
entries.content:
Afghanistan

Pakistan launches deadly airstrikes on Afghanistan

October 1, 2026

The Taliban government in Afghanistan said at least nine civilians were killed in Pakistani airstrikes on two provinces overnight. Pakistan said it had struck militant hideouts, killing 22 fighters.

Pakistan launched airstrikes overnight on two provinces in neighboring Afghanistan, the two countries said Thursday.

The Taliban government in Kabul said at least nine civilians, all women and children, were killed, while 11 others were wounded.

Pakistani authorities, on the other hand, said the strikes had killed 22 militants. Neither casualty toll could be independently verified.

The airstrikes are the latest clash between the two neighbors since cross-border tensions spiked earlier this year.

What do we know about the latest Pakistani airstrikes on Afghanistan?

The Afghan government spokesman said three civilian homes in the southern province of Helmand and in the eastern province of Kunar, which borders Pakistan, were hit, killing nine and injuring 11 others.

Residents of Helmand told the AFP news agency that three bombs had struck their village, and there is "no military or anything else" in the area.

"We condemn this act and consider this an act of aggression and a crime that violates all universally accepted principles," Zabihullah Mujahid said.

Authorities in Islamabad, however, said that 22 militants had been killed, and that weapons and ammunition had been destroyed.

The airstrikes on militant hideouts were "well planned and calibrated" and were carried out "with precision and accuracy," Pakistan's Ministry of Information said.

"Maximum precautions were taken and it was ensured that no collateral damage occurs," the statement said.

What's behind the conflict between Pakistan and Afghanistan?

The strikes overnight are the third time in the past two weeks that Pakistan has hit targets in Afghanistan.

Simmering tensions since the Taliban seized power in 2021 erupted into open conflict last year​​​​​​.

The two countries held peace talks in April to shore up a March truce, but sporadic flare-ups have continued in the months since.

Islamabad accuses the Taliban government in Kabul of harboring militants who carry out attacks across the border in Pakistan, an allegation Afghanistan denies.

"The threat to Pakistan emanates from Afghanistan," Pakistan's information ministry said. "Our action precisely targeted the terrorist hubs."

Since the conflict escalated last year, Pakistan has closed its border crossings with Afghanistan, which is heavily reliant on foreign food and humanitarian aid.    

Last week, the United Nations said more than 1,100 civilians had been killed or injured in Afghanistan as a result of the cross-border conflict this year.

Pakistan insists that it does not target civilians.

Edited by: Elizabeth Schumacher

entries.title: Cristiano Ronaldo walks out of Portugal camp
entries.summary: Cristiano Ronaldo has left Portugal’s camp after learning that he would not start the next Nations League match. Portugal's coach has denied reports of a rift between himself and the star player.
entries.content:
October 1, 2026

Cristiano Ronaldo has left Portugal’s camp after learning that he would not start the next Nations League match. Portugal's coach has denied reports of a rift between himself and the star player.

The 41-year-old forward left the Portugal camp on Wednesday after coach Jorge Jesus had told reporters at the Matchday-1 press conference that Cristiano Ronaldo would not feature in the starting lineup against Denmark in the Nations League.

The move comes amid reports of a rift between the Al-Nassr player and the coach, something that Jesus denied.

The 72-year-old coach conceded that his captain had been disappointed to remain on the bench in Portugal's win over Norway on Sunday, but he insisted that there had been "no incident whatsoever."

Ronaldo didn't explain why he had taken the decision, but in an Instagram post he said that "in time" he would "tell the Portuguese people the truth about the reasons" behind his departure.

"Following the national team coach's news conference, and after a conversation with the president of the Portuguese football federation, I decided to leave the national team's training camp," he said, adding that he had always "dedicated" himself to the national team.

"Now is the time to wish good luck to Portugal and to all my teammates, without exception."

For its part, the Portuguese federation (FPF) confirmed that the five-time Ballon d'Or winner had left the camp and that the team's preparations for Thursday's match in Copenhagen would continue without him.

"The entire delegation remains fully focused on the national team's upcoming fixtures and on achieving our goals," it said.

It wasn't immediately clear whether Ronaldo's departure would extend beyond the current international break.

In Wednesday's press conference, Jesus had said that Ronaldo would start on the bench and may be brought on as a sub.

"I don't know what's going to happen in the game," the coach said.

"If we need him to play, he'll play. If not, he won't."

Limited action

Ronaldo started Portugal's 1-0 win over Wales last Thursday but was substituted in the 67th minute. He was on the bench but saw no action in Sunday's 2-1 win over Norway in Oslo. Portugal face Norway again at home this coming Sunday.

Portugal leads Group A4 of the Nations League with six points from two matches, three points more than Denmark and Norway.

 Wednesday's news comes with Ronaldo's long-time rival Lionel Messi set to play his last match for Argentina next week. Earlier this year, Ronaldo, who is the all-time top goal scorer in men's competitive matches (979), had said recently that this Saudi Pro League season is likely to be the last of his professional career.

Earlier this year, he had said the 2026 World Cup would be his last but did not say exactly when he would retire from international football.

Edited by: Andreas Illmer

entries.title: Tennessee halts woman's execution after 'failed' attempt
entries.summary: Christa Pike was found alive and snoring, despite being administered two injections of a lethal drug. The state governor has ordered a review of the botched execution.
entries.content:
October 1, 2026

Christa Pike was found alive and snoring, despite being administered two injections of a lethal drug. The state governor has ordered a review of the botched execution.

The governor of Tennessee ordered a halt to the execution of Christa Gail Pike, convicted of murdering a schoolmate more than 30 years ago, after authorities "failed" to carry out her execution on Wednesday.

Despite being administered two doses of a lethal drug, Pike was found breathing.

The execution had been scheduled for 11:00 a.m. local time at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution. The injections were administered in front of witnesses, including journalists.

Pike, 50, was alive and loudly snoring after the attempted lethal injection and was taken to a hospital in an ambulance, her attorneys said.

She received treatment at the hospital, but authorities had not yet informed them about her condition, her attorneys added.

What do we know about the execution attempt?

Pike would have been the first woman executed in the southern US state of Tennessee in over 200 years.

According to media witnesses, who were observing from a separate room, Pike was strapped to a gurney.

"I'm going to leave this world the way I spent most of my life, and that is in love," she said in her "last" words.

By 8:26 p.m., witnesses reported that the second dose of pentobarbital had been given to Pike.

However, Pike was heard snoring behind the closed curtain until the microphone was cut off at 8:53 p.m.

At that time, media witnesses were asked to leave the room.

Tennessee orders investigation into failed execution of Christa Gail Pike

Governor Bill Lee said in a statement that he has ordered "a comprehensive, third-party review to determine exactly what occurred" and that scheduled executions will not be carried out this year.

"Carrying out a lawfully imposed sentence is among the State's most serious responsibilities, and the people of Tennessee expect it to be done in a manner that is not only legal and constitutional, but is effective," he said.

Pike's attorney filed an emergency motion late Wednesday with the Tennessee Supreme Court seeking to immediately halt and stay the execution.

In their appeal, they said she was in "unnecessary agony" and that it was violating her right to be executed free of cruel and unusual punishment.

This is the second time an execution has failed in Tennessee this year. In May, Tony Carruthers' execution by lethal injection failed.

"This event is the worst we've seen and unlike any other botched execution in the modern era," Robin Maher, the executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center, told the New York Times. "There is no precedent."

Pike was 18 when she and her boyfriend committed the murder she was convicted for.

"I was a mentally ill 18-year-old kid. It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I'd done," Pike had said in an earlier statement.

Edited by: Elizabeth Schumacher

entries.title: Germany news: Berlin leftists seek to pave way for coalition
entries.summary: The Berlin Left Party, Greens and SPD are to meet to clarify controversial issues ahead of possible coalition talks. The second fuel tax cut this year has come into force as gas and diesel prices spiral. DW has more.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Berlin leftists seek to pave way for coalition

Published October 1, 2026last updated October 1, 2026

The Berlin Left Party, Greens and SPD are to meet to clarify controversial issues ahead of possible coalition talks. The second fuel tax cut this year has come into force as gas and diesel prices spiral. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • The Left Party, the Greens and the Social Democrats (SPD) in Berlin are to test the ground for a possible coalition
  • Talks will center on accusations that the Left Party is antisemitic and has links to organized criminality, which it denies
  • A fuel tax cut aiming to reduce costs for motorists goes into effect for the second time this year

Here is a rundown of the stories from and about Germany that are hitting the headlines on Thursday, October 1, 2026:

f you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your preferred source on Google so you'll always see our verified news first.

Skip next section Ferry services suspended in part of Lake Constance

Ferry services suspended in part of Lake Constance

Low water levels in Lake Constance have forced boat services in one section of the waterway to be suspended, the municipal utility company in the southern German city of Konstanz said on Thursday.

The ferry operator, Bodensee-Schiffsbetriebe (BSB), has suspended services on the Untersee region until further notice, it said.

In a statement, BSB chief Frank Weber was cited as saying: "We have kept the ferry service running right down to the last centimeter. We have now reached the point where the risk of getting stuck in the harbor entrance has become too great."

The service had to be suspended to protect passengers and the ships, it continued.

The lake, which is known as the Bodensee in German, borders Germany, Austria and Switzerland.

The water gauge for the lake is currently measuring 251 cm (99 inches), 108 cm under the mean level of 359 cm for this day of the year as measured over many years.

A long period of dry weather has forced tourist and cargo ships in other waterways across Germany to reduce or suspend services.

Cargo shipping on the Rhine has been particularly affected, with negative consequences for several industries that depend on river-borne supplies of raw materials.

Skip next section IN DEPTH: Survey reveals Germans' greatest fear

IN DEPTH: Survey reveals Germans' greatest fear

An insurance company has carried out a survey to discover what people in Germany are most scared of.

And it is neither fascism, nor the climate crisis, nor spiders, nor Elon Musk, but — the cost of living.

Read our article to find out more: Germans' biggest fear is the high cost of living, an annual study finds

Skip next section Afghans denied entry despite Constitutional Court ruling

Afghans denied entry despite Constitutional Court ruling

 The German government has so far not granted entry to any Afghan nationals on a humanitarian list drawn up by the previous government, despite examining more than two dozen individual cases in keeping with a ruling by the Constitutional Court.

In response to a parliamentary question by Left Party politician Clara Bünger, the Interior Ministry said 25 cases had been examined since the court ruling on July 22, but all had been rejected.

After the Taliban retook power in Afghanistan in August 2021, the previous coalition government of Social Democrats (SPD), Greens and Free Democrats (FDP) had promised to grant entry to Afghan nationals who had worked for German institutions there or who were seen as endangered.

The current conservative-led government paused that program in May 2025 and in December 2025, the Interior Ministry rescinded all entry permissions that had been given under the scheme, saying there was "no political interest" in taking the people in.

The Federal Constitutional Court however ruled in July that Germany could not revoke the scheme en masse and that admission requests had to be considered on a case-to-case basis.   

Bünger called on the government "to take in the some 500 people still in question immediately and in an uncomplicated manner."

She said the fact that these Afghan nationals had been forced to live for years in fear and uncertainty was unjustifiable.

Skip next section Poland to extend controls on German border

Poland to extend controls on German border

Poland says it will extend controls along its border with Germany by six months until March 30 next year.

The Polish Interior Ministry said it would also be extending the measure, introduced in July 2025, on the border to Lithuania.

"Border controls are an effective tool ​for ⁠curbing illegal migration. Extending them will make ⁠it ​possible to manage migration pressure and strengthen border security," the ministry said in a statement.

Since the reintroduction of border controls, nearly 1,300 people have been denied entry into the ​country at ⁠the Lithuanian ​border and nearly ​1,200 at the German border, ​the statement said.

Germany has also had additional border controls in place at all its entry points since September 2024.

The border controls have been imposed even though Poland and Germany are members of the EU's Schengen Area, in which borders are theoretically meant to be open to allow seamless travel between EU members.

Under the Schengen Borders Code (SBC), member states are allowed to only temporarily reintroduce border controls in the case of security threats.

Both Poland and Germany have cited the threat of illegal immigration as having prompted the reinstatement of the controls.

Skip next section Fuel tax cut goes into force

Fuel tax cut goes into force

A three-month fuel tax cut went into effect in Germany at midnight on Wednesday, with motorists now likely to pay prices for gas and diesel that are lower by 16.7 cents (18.9 US cents) per liter in the coming weeks.

Prices before the cut went into effect were well over €2 per liter in most places, with September the most expensive month on record at the pump.

The same measure was introduced in Germany in May and June to give relief to motorists as fuel prices spiral largely as a result of the war in the Middle East.

The tax cut technically applies only to fuel leaving storage facilities or refineries, with gas stations not directly required to lower their prices.

However, prices at most filling stations are expected to fall quickly, as happened in May and June.

Critic of the measure say it reduces incentives to save fuel and will potentially not be passed on in full to all consumers.

Supporters say it is currently the best way to relieve the burden on motorists.

Skip next section NATO to receive German peace prize

NATO to receive German peace prize

 NATO is to be awarded with international Westphalian Peace Prize, worth €100,000 ($113,350), on Thursday afternoon, with Chancellor Friedrich Merz set to give the laudatory address.

The prize, which is expected to be received by NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte at the ceremony in Münster, honors the military alliance for its contribution to the European peace order.

The award is being presented to NATO at a time when its role as guarantor of Europe's security has been cast into some uncertainty by US ambivalence under the Trump administration.

The Westphalian Peace Price, which commemorates the Peace of Westphalia of 1648, is awarded every two years by the Economic Society for Westphalia and Lippe.

The 1648 peace agreement, concluded in the city halls of Münster and Osnabrück, ended the Thirty Years' War and is considered by many as a milestone in establishing the principle of national sovereignty.

Skip next section Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance changes its name

Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance changes its name

The populist Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) has officially dropped its founder's name from its title to become the Alliance for Social Justice and Economic Reason.

However, it will retain the abbreviation BSW.

Secretary general Oliver Ruhnert said Wagenknecht's name had initially been used because of her popularity but that the party had now succeeded in establishing itself as a brand in its own right.

Wagenknecht, a former parliamentary leader of the Left Party, founded the BSW in 2024, stepping down as its leader in November 2025.

Although the BSW advocates economic policies that are left-wing, it also has a nationalist and anti-migration stance that are more typical of the right-wing political spectrum, making it hard to classify in conventional terms.

It also favors closer ties with Russia.

Skip next section Suspected IS member arrested

Suspected IS member arrested

Federal police arrested a suspected member of the "Islamic State" (IS) terrorist group in central Germany on Wednesday morning. 

Prosecutors allege that the man joined the group in Iraq at the latest by early 2016, fighting in its ranks until early 2017.

He was detained in the Waldeck-Frankenberg district, north of Frankfurt, and is now being held in pre-trial detention after appearing at the Federal Court of Justice in Karlsruhe.

Skip next section Berlin Left Party, Greens and SPD meet for clarifying talks

Berlin Left Party, Greens and SPD meet for clarifying talks

Politicians from the socialist Left Party, the environmentalist Greens and the center-left Social Democrats (SPD) in Berlin are set to meet on Thursday to talk through several contentious issues before embarking on possible coalition negotiations.

Among other things, the talks will focus on accusations of antisemitism leveled at the Left Party, which won recent elections.

The party has also been accused of cultivating links to organized crime.

The accusations were fueled by the attendance by the head of an Arab clan with alleged criminal ties and a controversial pro-Palestinian activists at an election night event held by the Left Party in the Neukölln district of the city on September 20.

The Greens and the Left Party have said reaching agreement on these contentious issues is a "basic prerequisite" if formal exploratory talks on a coalition are to begin.

If the Left Party were to end up leading a coalition in the German capital, its lead candidate and parliamentary group co-leader, Elif Eralp, could become the first female governing mayor of Berlin.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

A hearty guten Tag from the DW newsroom in Bonn as the new month gets underway!

We will be looking at the pre-preliminary talks between the Left Party, the Greens and the Social Democrats (SPD) on possibly forming a coalition in the capital, Berlin.

The parties are approaching the matter with great caution amid accusations that the Left Party, which won recent elections, is antisemitic and maintains contacts with organized criminality.

This comes as another party, the populist Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), changes its name to the catchy "Alliance for Social Justice and Economic Reason", while retaining the BSW abbreviation.   

Meanwhile, motorists should be seeing prices at gas stations take a sudden fall as a fuel tax cut goes into effect.

Read on to find out more about these and other German stories.

entries.title: Swiss glaciers lose more than 5% in ice volume in 2026
entries.summary: Over the last five years, Swiss glaciers have lost nearly 20% of their mass, and 2026 saw the second-biggest loss of glacier volume on record. Experts warn there could be no ice left in the next 10-15 years.
entries.content:
October 1, 2026

Over the last five years, Swiss glaciers have lost nearly 20% of their mass, and 2026 saw the second-biggest loss of glacier volume on record. Experts warn there could be no ice left in the next 10-15 years.

Glaciers in Switzerland have lost nearly 20% of their mass in five years, experts said Thursday.

The experts said Swiss glaciers are melting rapidly and this year saw the second-biggest drop on record due to unprecedented heat waves in Europe.

There was a drop of 5.5% of Swiss glaciers this year, the Glacier Monitoring in Switzerland (GLAMOS) network found in a new study.

GLAMOS warns of total glacier loss

According to the report, over the past five years, the Swiss glaciers have lost almost ​a fifth of their ice, warning that in the future it could threaten water supplies.

The report also raised questions about the long-term survival of Europe's ice fields.

"Alpine glaciers have no chance of surviving in the long term under such conditions," said GLAMOS chief Matthias Huss. "The glaciers this year have lost enormous quantities of ice."

Little winter snowfall and record summer temperatures led Huss to call 2026 "a catastrophic year."

"This is a glacier that isn't surviving," he said. "There will probably be no ice in 10 or maybe 15 years."

The GLAMOS report reiterates concerns about the impact of global warming, especially in Europe, the world's fastest-warming continent.

"The warming that we are experiencing now can be attributed 100% to anthropogenic climate change. It's as simple as that," Huss said, using the term for climate change caused by human activity. "Without human emissions or fossil fuels we wouldn't have any warming at the moment."

entries.title: US military cuts generals, admirals by 20%, Hegseth says
entries.summary: The US defense secretary has also unveiled major changes, including a new drone command and an Elon Musk-led task force to assess the future of warfare.
entries.content:
United States of America

US military cuts generals, admirals by 20%, Hegseth says

October 1, 2026

The US defense secretary has also unveiled major changes, including a new drone command and an Elon Musk-led task force to assess the future of warfare.

US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced Wednesday that the United States military has slashed the number of its generals and admirals by 20%.

He made the announcement while addressing junior officers and enlisted leaders at the Marine Corps Base Quantico in Virginia during what he called his "State of the Force" address.

"The number-crunchers say we fired 10% of the generals and admirals across the force," Hegseth said, adding: "We've also reduced the overall number of general officer slots by an additional 10%."

"So yes, 20% reduction across the board," he noted. "The media calls that a purge. I call it accountability, and long overdue."

Cutting the fat or a purge?

The address came a year after a similar speech to top officers in which Hegseth said the US military was too fat, too focused on leftist "woke" ideas, and in need of major shake-up.

Since the start of Donald Trump's second term as president early last year, a number of top military personnel have been forced out of their positions.

Trump, for instance, fired the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, General Charles "CQ" Brown, without explanation in February 2025.

Other senior officers pushed out include the heads of the US Army, Navy and Coast Guard, the general who headed the National Security Agency, the vice chief of staff of the US Air Force, and a Navy admiral assigned to NATO.

Hegseth has insisted the president is simply choosing the military leaders he wants.

But Democratic lawmakers have raised concerns about the potential politicization of the US military.

Some members of Congress have called the latest cuts to the general ranks a "purge" that will take years to rebuild.

"He's got some kind of like deep-seated grievance about leadership in the military,” Democratic Senator Mark Kelly told the Associated Press. Kelly is a former Navy combat pilot who has been critical of Hegseth. "He's purging a generation of great leaders of the military, and it's going to take a generation to recover from it."

Republican Senator Mike Rounds, a member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, said he wanted to understand Hegseth's reasoning.

"If it's simply a matter of eliminating a very heavy top, there may be some validity to it, but I want to see it first," Rounds said.

What Hegseth said about the new command

On Wednesday, Hegseth also announced his intention to create a new drone-focused warfare command, which would oversee the rollout of autonomous and robotic capabilities.

He said that "the pace of war is changing faster than the process to support it."

The defense secretary pointed to Ukraine's use of drones to combat Russian forces to underscore how warfare and battlefield tactics are changing.

"Ukraine's lesson is not that one type of drone wins wars, but rather the need for a purpose-built system that maximizes the ability to adapt," Hegseth said.

To study the future of warfare, the secretary unveiled a task force led by tech billionaire Elon Musk, former Republican House Speaker Newt Gingrich and Palmer Luckey, co-founder of Anduril Industries.

He said the work "will be focused on discovering, developing and fielding the weapons and systems that our children and our grandchildren will need in their lifetimes." The Pentagon chief pointed to the need to dominate "any future battlefield, from under the Earth to beyond the moon."

entries.title: France: Hundreds arrested as student protests escalate
entries.summary: Student protests have grown in scale and intensity, with violent clashes in some places leading to hundreds of arrests and dozens of injuries.
entries.content:
France

France: Hundreds arrested as student protests escalate

October 1, 2026

Student protests have grown in scale and intensity, with violent clashes in some places leading to hundreds of arrests and dozens of injuries.

Security forces in France on Wednesday detained over 600 people as protests at high schools in parts of the country have intensified.   

Authorities said violent clashes and arson attacks have also left dozens of security personnel wounded.

Interior Minister Laurent Nunez condemned what he called an "escalation of violence" outside certain schools.

The violence left 83 police officers and gendarmes wounded on Wednesday, he said, adding that 32 teachers and pupils were also injured. The protests affected 356 schools, the minister noted.

He slammed the "targeting of law enforcement officers, the throwing of projectiles, acts of violence, verbal abuse, attempted arson, and what amounts... to urban violence."

Why are students protesting?

Teenagers at French lycées (equivalent to US high schools) have been blockading their schools since last week.

They are protesting overcrowded classes, heavy workloads, poor-quality learning materials and teacher shortages.

"There are cockroaches and rats everywhere in the school," Fadila, a 17-year-old student, told the Reuters news agency. She said temperatures in classrooms could swing from sweltering to below freezing, depending on the weather.

The movement began in the Ile-de-France region around the capital, Paris, but has since spread to other regions.

The cities worst affected Wednesday include Paris, Bordeaux in the southwest and Lyon in the southeast, and the northern city of Lille, where police again used tear gas in clashes, the AFP news agency reported.

What did the government say?

President Emmanuel Macron said the young people's concerns were legitimate but could in no way justify violence and attacks on police officers and teachers, among others.

"High schools are meant to be open and to share knowledge. They are not meant to be blockaded or to have trash ⁠cans set on fire," he told reporters in Madrid.

Both Macron and Nunez accused far-left groups of inciting violence during the protests.

"We observed that, in certain places, ⁠there were ​individuals acting as agitators — people who, moreover, moved from one school to another to stir ​up high school and other students and incite them to commit acts of violence," Nunez said.

Over the past few days, officials and politicians have denounced the left-wing La France Insoumise (France Unbowed or LFI) party and its presidential candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon for rhetoric they said was stoking students' anger.

On Monday, Melenchon had accused the government of implementing a "crackdown" with "obvious racist undertones."

"Hands off our youth!" he wrote on social media, while encouraging LFI activists and officials to support the protests wherever they could.

Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu called the accusation of racism "an insult" and accused Melenchon of "racializing a debate about student security and adding to division where a responsible politician should be looking to restore calm."
